// embassy/embassy-executor.me/src/raw/mod.rs
pub struct TaskStorage<F: Future + 'static> {
    raw: TaskHeader,
    future: UninitCell<F>, // Valid if STATE_SPAWNED
    
    // Future generated by an async block or function is represented in memory as a Stack-Allocated State Machine 
    // (an enum).
    // Because async functions can "pause" at .await points, the Future must store all variables that are "alive" 
    // across those points so they can be restored when the future is polled again.
    // 1. The "Enum" Structure
    // Internally, the compiler transforms your code into a structure that looks like a hidden enum. Each variant 
    // represents a state between two .await points.
    // Logical representation of a Future's memory layout
    // enum MyFutureState {
    //     Start { arg1: i32 },                       // Initial state
    //     WaitingForTimer { timer_ref: Timer },      // Variables alive during 1st .await
    //     WaitingForUart { data_buffer: [u8; 32] },  // Variables alive during 2nd .await
    //     Done,                                      // Final state
    // 2. What is inside the Future's memory?
    // The size of a Future (and thus the size of its TaskStorage in Embassy) is determined by the largest set of 
    // variables held at any single .await point:
    // - Captured Arguments: Any data passed into the async fn.
    // - Local Variables: Any variable defined in the function that is used after an .await call.
    // - Sub-Futures: If you call another_async_fn().await, the memory for that function's future is embedded inside 
    //   yours.
    // - The State Discriminant: A small integer (usually 1 byte) that tells the poll function which state it is 
    //   currently in.
    // 3. Self-Referential Pointers (The "Pin" Requirement)
    // This is the most critical part for ESP32-C3 development. If you create a reference to a local variable and 
    // then .await:
    // async fn my_task() {
    //     let x = 10;
    //     let x_ref = &x; // This reference points to memory inside the Future itself!
    //     timer.wait().await;
    //     println!("{}", x_ref);
    // }
    // The memory layout now contains a pointer (x_ref) that points to another spot in the same struct (x).
    // - This makes the Future self-referential.
    // - If you move the Future in memory, x_ref would point to the "old" location, causing a crash.
    // - This is why Embassy uses UninitCell and write_in_place: It ensures the Future is born at a specific address 
    //   in static memory and never moves, satisfying the requirements of Pin.
    // 4. Representation in embassy-executor
    // In TaskStorage<F>, the Future F is laid out exactly as described above within the UninitCell.
    // - Size: The compiler calculates the exact size of F at compile time.
    // - Alignment: The Future is aligned according to the strictest alignment requirement of any of its internal 
    //   variables (e.g., if it contains a u32, the whole Future struct is 4-byte aligned).
}



impl<F: Future + 'static> TaskStorage<F> {
    const NEW: Self = Self::new();

    /// Create a new TaskStorage, in not-spawned state.
    // 182
    pub const fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            raw: TaskHeader {
                state: State::new(),
                run_queue_item: RunQueueItem::new(),
                executor: AtomicPtr::new(core::ptr::null_mut()),
                // Note: this is lazily initialized so that a static `TaskStorage` will go in `.bss`
                poll_fn: SyncUnsafeCell::new(None),

                timer_queue_item: TimerQueueItem::new(),

                #[cfg(feature = "trace")]
                name: None,
                #[cfg(feature = "trace")]
                id: 0,
                #[cfg(feature = "trace")]
                all_tasks_next: AtomicPtr::new(core::ptr::null_mut()),
            },
            future: UninitCell::uninit(),
        }
    }
    // state, run/timer_queue_item, executor:
    // the difference in synchronization primitives for TaskHeader fields is driven by the complexity of the operations 
    // performed on each field and the nature of the shared data
    // The reference to the executor is stored as an AtomicPtr because it represents a static, read-mostly pointer that 
    // does not change its internal state through the header.
    // - Simple Assignment: Once a task is spawned, it is associated with a specific executor. Setting or reading this 
    //   pointer is a single atomic operation that doesn't require complex logic or multi-step validation.
    // - No Interior Mutability Needed: The TaskHeader only needs to know which executor it belongs to so it can enqueue 
    //   itself. It doesn't modify the executor's internal structures directly through this pointer in a way that 
    //   requires a lock at the header level.
    // - Efficiency: Atomic operations are significantly faster than Mutexes because they avoid the overhead of 
    //   disabling interrupts or managing lock states. Although in case of esp32c3 AtomicPtr finally implemented via 
    //   CriticalSection, but embassy is for general cases
    // The state and run_queue_item require a Mutex (specifically a RawMutex like CriticalSectionRawMutex) because they 
    // involve complex, multi-step state transitions that must be perfectly synchronized across thread levels (e.g., 
    // Thread mode vs. Interrupts).
    // - Atomicity of State Transitions: The state isn't just a single value; it tracks multiple flags (e.g., spawned, 
    //   woken, running). A change often requires checking one flag before setting another. A Mutex ensures these 
    //   "check-and-set" operations are atomic, preventing race conditions where two interrupts might wake a task 
    //   simultaneously.
    // - Linked List Integrity (run_queue_item): The run_queue_item is typically part of a linked list used by the 
    //   executor's run queue.
    //   - Adding or removing a task from a linked list involves updating multiple pointers (the task's own pointers 
    //     and those of its neighbors).
    //   - If an interrupt (Waker) tries to enqueue a task while the executor is currently dequeueing it, a simple 
    //     atomic pointer wouldn't be enough to prevent the list from becoming corrupted.
    // - Critical Sections: Embassy often runs in environments without an OS, where "locking" a Mutex actually means 
    //   disabling interrupts. This is necessary to ensure that a high-priority interrupt doesn't modify the task's 
    //   queue status while the low-priority executor loop is in the middle of processing it. 
    //
    // const NEW: Self = Self::new();
    // the compiler knows the size of the future at compile time through a process called monomorphization. Even 
    // though TaskStorage::new is a const function, it is generic over the type F of the future.
    // 1. Monomorphization
    // When you use the #[embassy_executor::task] macro, the Rust compiler generates a concrete version of the 
    // TaskStorage<F> struct for every specific async function (future) you define.
    // - Every async function in Rust is transformed into its own unique, unnamed type F that implements Future.
    // - The size of this type F is determined by the local variables and state needed for that specific async function.
    // - When the compiler encounters TaskStorage<MySpecificFutureType>, it creates a specific version of that struct 
    //   where UninitCell<F> is replaced with the exact size required by MySpecificFutureType.
    // 2. UninitCell and MaybeUninit
    // The UninitCell<F> is a wrapper around MaybeUninit<F>. In Rust, MaybeUninit<T> is a special type that:
    // - Always has the exact same size and alignment as the underlying type T.
    // - Tells the compiler to reserve that space but not to track whether it is initialized or call its destructor 
    //   automatically.
    // - Because F must implement the Sized trait (which is the default for generic parameters), the compiler ensures 
    //   its size is known at compile time. 
    // 3. Static Allocation via Macros
    // The #[embassy_executor::task] macro automates the creation of a static instance of this TaskStorage.
    // Nightly _EmbassyInternalTaskTrait to calculate the exact size of each task's future and allocate it in a 
    // dedicated static block:
    // trait _EmbassyInternalTaskTrait
    //     type Fut: ::core::future::Future<Output: #embassy_executor::_export::TaskReturnValue> + 'static;
    //     fn construct(#fargs) -> Self::Fut;
    // impl _EmbassyInternalTaskTrait for ()
    //     type Fut = impl core::future::Future<Output: #embassy_executor::_export::TaskReturnValue> + 'static;
    //     fn construct(#fargs) -> Self::Fut
    //         #task_inner_ident(#(#full_args,)*)
    // ...
    // static POOL: #embassy_executor::raw::TaskPool<<() as _EmbassyInternalTaskTrait>::Fut, POOL_SIZE> = 
    //     #embassy_executor::raw::TaskPool::new();
    // 
    // pub struct TaskPool<F: Future + 'static, const N: usize> {
    //     pool: [TaskStorage<F>; N],
    // }
    //
    // unsafe { POOL.#spawn(move || <() as _EmbassyInternalTaskTrait>::construct(#(#full_args,)*)) }
    //
    // Why const works in "const NEW: Self = Self::new();"
    // A const function can be generic. When TaskStorage::<F>::new() is called in a static context:
    // 1. The compiler identifies the concrete type F.
    // 2. It calculates sizeof(F).
    // 3 It allocates the static memory based on that size.
    //   The UninitCell::uninit() call inside is simply a "no-op" for the bytes; it tells the compiler "don't fill 
    //   these bytes with anything yet," but the amount of space reserved is strictly defined by the type F. 
    //
    // poll_fn: SyncUnsafeCell::new(None) is the most simple way to hold an option whics is interior mutable and sync
    // for the static TaskHeader
    // bit it is a manual monomorphization, since every taskstorage's future get an individual poll_fn, which is the
    // same code (see AvailableTask::initialize_impl below)
    // BUT 
    // In the Embassy executor, storing a function pointer like TaskStorage::poll in the TaskHeader is a technique 
    // for Type Erasure. Even though the code is monomorphized into specific future types, the executor needs a way 
    // to handle many different task types uniformly.
    // Here is why this design is used:
    // 1. Heterogeneous Run Queue
    // The executor maintains a single run queue (a linked list) of tasks that are ready to be executed. 
    // - In your application, you might have a blink_task, a sensor_task, and a network_task. Each of these is a 
    //   unique, different Rust type.
    // - The run queue stores *mut TaskHeader. Because TaskHeader is a common "base" struct at the start of every 
    //   TaskStorage<F>, the executor can point to any task regardless of its internal Future type F.
    // - Without a function pointer, the executor would need to know the exact type of every task in the list at 
    //   compile time, which is impossible for a dynamic list of mixed tasks. 
    // - Without a function pointer, the executor would need to know the exact type of every task in the list at 
    //   compile time, which is impossible for a dynamic list of mixed tasks.
    // 2. Manual Virtual Dispatch (Avoiding dyn)
    // Normally, you would use a trait object (dyn Future) to handle different types. However, dyn Trait has downsides 
    // in embedded systems:
    // - No Alloc: Trait objects often require a heap (Box<dyn Future>), which Embassy avoids entirely.
    // - Binary Size: dyn can bring in large vtables and complex metadata.
    // - The Solution: Storing a simple function pointer (fn(*mut TaskHeader)) is a "manual" form of polymorphism. 
    //   It allows the executor to simply call (header.poll_fn)(header). 
    // 3. Bridging Monomorphization and Runtime
    // While it's true that TaskStorage<F>::poll is monomorphized (a unique version is generated for every F), the 
    // executor loop is not monomorphized for every task combination.
    // - The macro creates a unique TaskStorage<F> and a unique poll function for your task.
    // - During spawn, the address of that specific poll function is saved into the TaskHeader.
    // - The executor just sees a list of TaskHeader pointers. When it pops one, it doesn't know if it's the blinker 
    //   or the sensor—it just calls the stored poll_fn, which "knows" how to cast the header back to the correct 
    //   TaskStorage<F> and poll the internal future. 
    //
    // While monomorphization creates unique poll functions for every task, the binary size overhead is minimized 
    // through several advanced compiler and framework techniques. 
    // 1. Link-Time Optimization (LTO)
    // Enabling LTO (specifically lto = "fat") is the most effective way to save on this overhead. 
    // - Deduplication: If two different tasks have futures with similar logic (even if their types are technically 
    //   different), the compiler's LTO pass can identify identical machine code blocks across monomorphized functions 
    //   and merge them into one.
    // - Inlining: LTO allows the compiler to inline the small TaskStorage::poll wrapper directly into the executor's 
    //   call site if it determines that doing so saves more space than keeping the function pointer.
    // 2. "Outer" vs. "Inner" Function Splitting
    // To prevent huge code bloat, Embassy and the Rust compiler often use a pattern where:
    // - The generic "outer" function (TaskStorage::poll) is kept very small—it only performs the unsafe cast and 
    //   calls the future's poll.
    // - The non-generic "inner" logic (the actual async state machine) is what contains the bulk of the code. This 
    //   ensures that only the truly unique logic of your task is replicated, while the "boilerplate" for the executor 
    //   remains minimal. 
    // 4. Configuration for Minimal Size
    // You can further reduce the impact of these monomorphized tasks by adjusting your Cargo.toml:
    // - codegen-units = 1: Forces the compiler to process the entire crate as a single unit, which maximizes the 
    // chances for the deduplication mentioned above.
    // - opt-level = "z" or "s": Specifically tells the compiler to prioritize binary size over execution speed. 
}


pub struct AvailableTask<F: Future + 'static> {
    task: &'static TaskStorage<F>,
}

impl<F: Future + 'static> AvailableTask<F> {
    /// Try to claim a [`TaskStorage`].
    ///
    /// This function returns `None` if a task has already been spawned and has not finished running.
    pub fn claim(task: &'static TaskStorage<F>) -> Option<Self> {
        // If task is idle, mark it as spawned + run_queued and return true
        task.raw.state.spawn().then(|| Self { task })
    }

    // 280
    fn initialize_impl<S>(self, future: impl FnOnce() -> F) -> SpawnToken<S> {
        unsafe {
            self.task.raw.poll_fn.set(Some(TaskStorage::<F>::poll));
            self.task.future.write_in_place(future);

            let task = TaskRef::new(self.task);

            SpawnToken::new(task)
        }
    }
    // The SpawnToken<S> and the FnOnce() -> F work together to solve the "static future" problem in a 
    // memory-safe and thread-safe way. Here is the breakdown of why this specific implementation uses 
    // those two mechanisms:
    // 1. Postponed Evaluation: future.write_in_place(future)
    // In standard Rust, when you call an async fn, it returns the Future object immediately. If that future 
    // is !Send, it is stuck on the current thread. A future can be !Send if it captured a !Send resource  
    // (like a peripheral handle bound to a core).
    // By passing an impl FnOnce() -> F (the closure) instead of the future F:
    // - Zero-Copy Initialization: The future F is created directly inside the static memory of the TaskStorage via 
    //   write_in_place. This avoids a "move" of the future itself, which is critical for futures that might be large 
    //   or self-referential.
}

pub struct TaskPool<F: Future + 'static, const N: usize> {
    pool: [TaskStorage<F>; N],
}

impl<F: Future + 'static, const N: usize> TaskPool<F, N> {
    pub const fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            pool: [TaskStorage::NEW; N],
        }
    }
    // see the explanation above at TaskStorage::new

    /// Try to spawn a task in the pool.
    ///
    /// See [`TaskStorage::spawn()`] for details.
    ///
    /// This will loop over the pool and spawn the task in the first storage that
    /// is currently free. If none is free, a "poisoned" SpawnToken is returned,
    /// which will cause [`Spawner::spawn()`](super::Spawner::spawn) to return the error.
    // 348
    fn spawn_impl<T>(&'static self, future: impl FnOnce() -> F) -> SpawnToken<T> {
        match self.pool.iter().find_map(AvailableTask::claim) {
            Some(task) => task.initialize_impl::<T>(future),
            None => SpawnToken::new_failed(),
        }
    }

    /// Like spawn(), but allows the task to be send-spawned if the args are Send even if
    /// the future is !Send.
    ///
    /// Not covered by semver guarantees. DO NOT call this directly. Intended to be used
    /// by the Embassy macros ONLY.
    ///
    /// SAFETY: `future` must be a closure of the form `move || my_async_fn(args)`, where `my_async_fn`
    /// is an `async fn`, NOT a hand-written `Future`.
    // 374
    pub unsafe fn _spawn_async_fn<FutFn>(&'static self, future: FutFn) -> SpawnToken<impl Sized>
    where
        FutFn: FnOnce() -> F,
    {
        // See the comment in AvailableTask::__initialize_async_fn for explanation.
        self.spawn_impl::<FutFn>(future)
    }
    // This function addresses a common "bottleneck" in Rust’s async trait system regarding where a future is created 
    // versus where it is stored. The core of the trick lies in the difference between the Closure/Function (FutFn) 
    // and the Future (F) it produces.
    // 1. The Conflict: Send vs. !Send
    // Embassy tasks are stored in static TaskStorage, which is Sync but contains !Send internal headers to "pin" the 
    // task to a specific executor core or interrupt level.
    // - The Problem: If a future F is !Send, you normally cannot pass it across a thread boundary to a different
    //   executor.
    // - The Goal: You want to be able to call spawner.spawn(...) from Thread A to start a task on Executor B, even if 
    //   the resulting task/future is !Sync + !Send.
    // 2. How _spawn_async_fn Solves It
    // Instead of taking a pre-created Future, this function takes a Closure/Function (FutFn: FnOnce() -> F).
    // - The Closure is Send: As long as the arguments you captured in the closure (the "args") are Send, the closure 
    //   itself is Send.
    // - Cross-Thread Transport: Because the closure is Send, the SpawnToken and the closure can be safely passed from 
    //   the caller's thread to the Executor's thread.
    // - In-Place Initialization: The future F is not created yet. It is only created inside the static TaskStorage on 
    //   the destination executor's thread when the executor calls future().
    // 3. "Send-Spawned" vs. "Send-Future"
    // - Without this function: You would have to create the future first. If the future captured a !Send resource 
    //   (like a peripheral handle bound to a core), the future would be !Send. You couldn't move it to the executor.
    // - With this function: You move the instructions (the closure) and the data (the args). Since the data is Send, 
    //   the move is legal. The !Send future is then born directly inside its final, static home on the destination 
    //   thread.
    // 4. Why the impl Sized?
    // The SpawnToken<impl Sized> is an opaque handle. It represents the "reservation" in the TaskStorage. By keeping 
    // it Sized and not exposing the internal future type F directly, Embassy can manage the memory requirements of 
    // the task arena without leaking complex, self-referential future types into your application code.
    // Summary
    // This function allows you to spawn a task on a different core or interrupt level by moving the "recipe" 
    // (the closure) and "ingredients" (the args) across the boundary, rather than trying to move the "finished cake" 
    // (the initialized future), which might be too fragile or "sticky" (!Send) to move. 
}

// embassy/embassy-executor.me/src/spawner.rs
/// Token to spawn a newly-created task in an executor.
pub struct SpawnToken<S> {
    raw_task: Option<raw::TaskRef>,
    phantom: PhantomData<*mut S>,
}
// SpawnToken<S> uses PhantomData<*mut S> as a compile-time "marker" to tie the thread-safety of the token to the 
// thread-safety of the task's arguments (S).
// Here is how it enforces those rules:
// 1. The Role of PhantomData<*mut S>
// PhantomData<T> acts as if the struct contains a value of type T for the purposes of the compiler's auto-trait 
// analysis.
// - Auto-Traits: In Rust, a struct is automatically Send if all its fields are Send.
// - Raw Pointers: The type *mut S is never Send or Sync, regardless of what S is.
// - Consequence: Because SpawnToken<S> contains a *mut S marker, the SpawnToken itself becomes !Send (not Send). 
//   This means the token cannot be moved to another thread on its own.
// 2. Enforcing Send via Function Bounds
// The real magic happens in the spawn methods of the two different spawner types:
// - SendSpawner::spawn<S: Send>(token: SpawnToken<S>):
//   - This method has a trait bound requiring S: Send.
//   - If your task arguments (S) are not Send, you cannot call this method. The compiler will reject it because the 
//     SpawnToken<S> you have doesn't satisfy the S: Send requirement.
//   - Because SendSpawner itself is Send, it can be sent to other threads (like an interrupt handler), but it can only 
//     "accept" tokens where the underlying data is safe to cross that thread boundary.
// - Spawner::spawn<S>(token: SpawnToken<S>):
//   - This method does not have a Send bound on S.
//   - It can accept any SpawnToken<S>, even if the arguments are not thread-safe.
//   - The Safety Catch: The Spawner struct itself is marked as !Send. You cannot move the Spawner to another thread.
//   - Since you can't move the Spawner and you can't move the SpawnToken (due to the *mut S pointer marker), both 
//     must stay on the current thread, ensuring the non-Send data is never accessed incorrectly. 
// 3. How SendSpawner accepts a !Send SpawnToken
// The SendSpawner can accept a SpawnToken<S> because the token is passed by value into its spawn method.
// - The Spawner moves to the Token: Since SendSpawner is Send, you can send the spawner handle to the thread where 
//   the SpawnToken was created.
// - Local Consumption: You then call send_spawner.spawn(token) on that same thread. The !Send token never actually 
//   crosses a thread boundary; it is consumed exactly where it was born.
// - The Bound Check: The SendSpawner::spawn<S: Send>(...) method has a strict trait bound. Even though you are calling 
//   it locally, the compiler checks if the task's arguments (S) are Send. If they are not, the code will not compile. 
// 4. Why this ensures safety
// This design forces a "meeting" between the spawner and the token while maintaining strict safety rules:
// - For Spawner (Non-Send): It can spawn anything because it is pinned to the executor's thread. It never "sends" 
//   data anywhere else, so S doesn't need to be Send.
// - For Spawner (Non-Send): It can spawn anything because it is pinned to the executor's thread. It never "sends" data 
//   anywhere else, so S doesn't need to be Send.
//   - Even if you consume the token "locally" on Thread A, the executor on Thread B will eventually run that task.
//   - If the data inside (S) were not Send, the executor on Thread B would be accessing thread-unsafe data from 
//     Thread A, causing a race condition.
//   The S: Send bound on the spawn method prevents this. 
// 5. Summary of the Flow
// - Call Task: You get a SpawnToken<S>. It is !Send and cannot leave the current thread.
// - Get Spawner: You use a SendSpawner (which can travel between threads).
// - Spawn: You bring the SendSpawner to the thread holding the SpawnToken.
// - Verification: The compiler sees you are using a SendSpawner. It looks at the SpawnToken<S> and asks: "Is S safe 
//   to be sent to the executor's thread?"
//   - If Yes (S: Send), the spawn succeeds.
//   - If No, the compiler blocks the call, even though the token itself didn't move. 

/// Handle to spawn tasks into an executor.
pub struct Spawner {
    executor: &'static raw::Executor,
    not_send: PhantomData<*mut ()>,
}
// the Spawner struct uses PhantomData<*mut ()> primarily to enforce thread-safety rules by making the struct 
// !Send (not Send) and !Sync (not Sync).
// The Spawner is designed to spawn tasks on a specific executor. 
// - The Rule: A standard Spawner can only be used on the thread where its associated executor is running. This allows 
//   it to safely spawn non-Send tasks (tasks that contain data which cannot safely move between threads).
// - The Mechanism: By adding a field of type PhantomData<*mut ()>, Embassy uses a "marker." In Rust, raw pointers 
//   like *mut () are neither Send nor Sync.
// - The Result: Because Spawner "contains" this non-thread-safe marker, the compiler automatically marks the entire 
//   Spawner struct as !Send and !Sync. This prevents you from accidentally sending a Spawner to another thread or 
//   interrupt handler where it could cause memory unsafety.

impl Spawner {
    pub fn spawn<S>(&self, token: SpawnToken<S>) -> Result<(), SpawnError> {
        let task = token.raw_task;
        mem::forget(token);

        match task {
            Some(task) => {
                unsafe { self.executor.spawn(task) };
                Ok(())
            }
            None => Err(SpawnError::Busy),
        }
    }
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
pub(crate) struct Pender(*mut ());

unsafe impl Send for Pender {}
unsafe impl Sync for Pender {}

impl Pender {
    pub(crate) fn pend(self) {
        extern "Rust" {
            fn __pender(context: *mut ());
        }
        unsafe { __pender(self.0) };
    }
}

pub(crate) struct SyncExecutor {
    run_queue: RunQueue,
    pender: Pender,
}

impl SyncExecutor {
    pub(crate) fn new(pender: Pender) -> Self {
        Self {
            run_queue: RunQueue::new(),
            pender,
        }
    }

    /// Enqueue a task in the task queue
    ///
    /// # Safety
    /// - `task` must be a valid pointer to a spawned task.
    /// - `task` must be set up to run in this executor.
    /// - `task` must NOT be already enqueued (in this executor or another one).
    #[inline(always)]
    unsafe fn enqueue(&self, task: TaskRef, l: state::Token) {
        #[cfg(feature = "trace")]
        trace::task_ready_begin(self, &task);

        if self.run_queue.enqueue(task, l) {
            self.pender.pend();
        }
    }

    pub(super) unsafe fn spawn(&'static self, task: TaskRef) {
        task.header()
            .executor
            .store((self as *const Self).cast_mut(), Ordering::Relaxed);

        #[cfg(feature = "trace")]
        trace::task_new(self, &task);

        state::locked(|l| {
            self.enqueue(task, l);
        })
    }

    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// Same as [`Executor::poll`], plus you must only call this on the thread this executor was created.
    pub(crate) unsafe fn poll(&'static self) {
        #[cfg(feature = "trace")]
        trace::poll_start(self);

        self.run_queue.dequeue_all(|p| {
            let task = p.header();

            #[cfg(feature = "trace")]
            trace::task_exec_begin(self, &p);

            // Run the task
            task.poll_fn.get().unwrap_unchecked()(p);

            #[cfg(feature = "trace")]
            trace::task_exec_end(self, &p);
        });

        #[cfg(feature = "trace")]
        trace::executor_idle(self)
    }
}

/// Raw executor.
///
/// This is the core of the Embassy executor. It is low-level, requiring manual
/// handling of wakeups and task polling. If you can, prefer using one of the
/// [higher level executors](crate::Executor).
///
/// The raw executor leaves it up to you to handle wakeups and scheduling:
///
/// - To get the executor to do work, call `poll()`. This will poll all queued tasks (all tasks
///   that "want to run").
/// - You must supply a pender function, as shown below. The executor will call it to notify you
///   it has work to do. You must arrange for `poll()` to be called as soon as possible.
/// - Enabling `arch-xx` features will define a pender function for you. This means that you
///   are limited to using the executors provided to you by the architecture/platform
///   implementation. If you need a different executor, you must not enable `arch-xx` features.
///
/// The pender can be called from *any* context: any interrupt priority level, etc.
/// It may be called synchronously from any `Executor` method call as well.
/// You must deal with this correctly.
///
/// In particular, you must NOT call `poll` directly from the pender callback, as this violates
/// the requirement for `poll` to not be called reentrantly.
///
/// The pender function must be exported with the name `__pender` and have the following signature:
///
/// ```rust
/// #[export_name = "__pender"]
/// fn pender(context: *mut ()) {
///    // schedule `poll()` to be called via the static SIGNAL_WORK_THREAD_MODE
///    // or in multi_core via SoftwareInterrupt
///
///
/// }
/// ```
///
/// The `context` argument is a piece of arbitrary data the executor will pass to the pender.
/// You can set the `context` when calling [`Executor::new()`]. You can use it to, (((for example,
/// differentiate between executors))), or to pass a pointer to a callback that should be called.
// 501
#[repr(transparent)]
pub struct Executor {
    pub(crate) inner: SyncExecutor,

    _not_sync: PhantomData<*mut ()>,
}
// Pender is the low-level mechanism (usually a software interrupt or a specific bit-set) that signals the hardware 
// to "wake up" the executor so it can poll its tasks.
// When the documentation states that the pender may be called synchronously from any Executor method, it means:
// 1. Re-entrancy and Immediate Execution
// If an Executor method (like spawning a task or waking a task) is currently running on the CPU, it might trigger 
// the pender immediately before that method even returns.
// - The "Pender" function doesn't just queue a request for later; it performs the "poke" to the system right then 
//   and there.
// - Safety Implication: The Pender implementation must be safe to call even if the Executor is currently in the middle 
//   of modifying its internal state. This is why the Pender is typically a very simple, atomic operation (like setting 
//   a bit in a register).
// 2. No Context Switching Required
// Calling it "synchronously" implies the signal is sent from the current execution context.
// - If you call spawner.spawn(...) from a high-priority interrupt, the Pender will be called immediately from within 
//   that interrupt.
// - It does not "wait" for a thread-mode context switch or a specific "safe point."
// 3. Avoiding Deadlocks
// Because it can be called synchronously from any method, the Pender must not attempt to acquire any locks that the 
// Executor itself might already be holding.
// - If the Executor holds a lock and calls the Pender, and the Pender tries to take that same lock, the system will 
//   deadlock.
// - This is why the Pender in the ESP32-C3 is usually a simple Software Interrupt (SWINT) trigger. It just flips a 
//   hardware flag that causes an interrupt to fire later (or immediately if priorities allow).
// 4. Integration with the ESP32-C3
// - The Executor might be running in the main loop.
// - You call spawn.
// - The Executor calls the Pender.
// - The Pender triggers a Machine Software Interrupt (MSIP).
// - Because this happened synchronously, the MSIP is now pending. As soon as the spawn call finishes and interrupts 
//   are enabled, the CPU will jump to the Executor's polling routine.
// Summary
// The statement is a warning to developers of Pender implementations: Your pend() function must be "re-entrant" and 
// extremely fast, because the Executor will call it at any time, even while the Executor's own internal data is being 
// modified. It ensures that the Executor is "poked" as soon as there is new work, regardless of where that work came 
// from.

impl Executor {
    pub(crate) unsafe fn wrap(inner: &SyncExecutor) -> &Self {
        mem::transmute(inner)
    }
    // 1 The Pender Specialization
    // The most important "architecture-specific" part of the executor is the Pender (in SyncExecutor).
    // - In embassy-executor, the high-level Executor struct is defined in src/arch/*.rs (e.g., riscv.rs or cortex_m.rs).
    // - For ESP32-C3 (RISC-V): When you enable the arch-riscv feature, the Executor is initialized with a specific 
    //   Pender implementation that knows how to wake up a RISC-V core. On the ESP32-C3, this typically uses a Machine 
    //   Software Interrupt (MSIP) or a specific bit in the mstatus register.
    // - How it becomes specific: The SyncExecutor (inner) accepts a Pender as a generic parameter. The Executor (outer) 
    //   "closes" that generic by providing the architecture's specific pend function.
    // 2. The run() Loop and Sleep Instructions
    // The specialization isn't in the data it holds, but in the assembly instructions executed in its run() loop.
    // - Cortex-M: Uses the WFE (Wait For Event) and SEV (Set Event) instructions.
    // - Cortex-M: Uses the WFE (Wait For Event) and SEV (Set Event) instructions.
    // 3. The #[embassy_executor::main] Macro
    // - When you write #[embassy_executor::main], the macro detects your target architecture.
    // - For ESP32-C3, it expands into code that specifically imports embassy_executor::Executor from the RISC-V module.
    // - It also handles the bootstrapping of the Timer Queue, which on the ESP32-C3 is specialized to use the 
    //   hardware's System Timer (Systimer).

    /// Create a new executor.
    ///
    /// When the executor has work to do, it will call the pender function and pass `context` to it.
    ///
    /// See [`Executor`] docs for details on the pender.
    // 518
    pub fn new(context: *mut ()) -> Self {
        Self {
            inner: SyncExecutor::new(Pender(context)),
            _not_sync: PhantomData,
        }
    }
    // Primarily used to implement Custom or Multi-instance Executors, specifically those that run at different interrupt 
    // priorities (preemptive multitasking).
    // While fn wrap is used to create the default, single-core "Thread Mode" executor from a static SyncExecutor, 
    // Executor::new is required for the following advanced scenarios:
    // 1. The Purpose of the context Pointer
    // The context argument is a piece of arbitrary data (*mut ()) that the executor passes to the pender function 
    // (__pender). 
    // - When a task on that executor is woken, the executor calls the pender.
    // - By passing a specific context during Executor::new(), you allow the pender to distinguish between multiple 
    //   executors.
    // - Example: On the ESP32-C3, if you have two executors, the context could be a pointer to the specific Machine 
    //   Software Interrupt (MSIP) register or the specific Interrupt Number that should be triggered to wake that 
    //   executor. 
    // 2. Implementing InterruptExecutor
    // The most common use case for Executor::new is within the implementation of an Interrupt Mode Executor. 
    // - Unlike the default Thread Mode executor (which usually has a fixed context or uses architecture-specific 
    //   instructions like wfi), an InterruptExecutor needs to know which interrupt it is tied to.
    // - The InterruptExecutor's constructor will call raw::Executor::new(interrupt_id as *mut ()) so that the pender 
    //   knows exactly which interrupt to "pend" (trigger) when work is ready.
    // 3. Running Tasks at Different Priorities
    // Embassy projects often use multiple executors to allow high-priority tasks to preempt lower-priority ones.
    // - Thread Mode Executor: Created via the main macro (which uses wrap).
    // - Interrupt Executor(s): Created manually in your code using new(). These executors run inside an interrupt 
    // handler, allowing them to interrupt the Thread Mode executor. 
    //
    // In short: You use Executor::new when you need to define where and how the wake-up signal should be sent (e.g., 
    // to a specific interrupt), whereas wrap is used for the standard "default" executor where the wake-up mechanism 
    // is already globally defined by the architecture.

    pub(super) unsafe fn spawn(&'static self, task: TaskRef) {
        self.inner.spawn(task)
    }

    pub unsafe fn poll(&'static self) {
        self.inner.poll()
    }

    pub fn spawner(&'static self) -> super::Spawner {
        super::Spawner::new(self)
    }
}

// continued TaskStorage implementation
// this is the task's future's poll, which is the standard poll, which is always set to poll_fn,
// which is called by the executor poll
impl<F: Future + 'static> TaskStorage<F> {
unsafe fn poll(p: TaskRef) {
        let this = &*p.as_ptr().cast::<TaskStorage<F>>();

        let future = Pin::new_unchecked(this.future.as_mut());
        let waker = waker::from_task(p);
        let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&waker);

        // polls the task's future
        match future.poll(&mut cx) {
            Poll::Ready(_) => {
                #[cfg(feature = "trace")]
                let exec_ptr: *const SyncExecutor = this.raw.executor.load(Ordering::Relaxed);

                // As the future has finished and this function will not be called
                // again, we can safely drop the future here.
                this.future.drop_in_place();

                // We replace the poll_fn with a despawn function, so that the task is cleaned up
                // when the executor polls it next.
                this.raw.poll_fn.set(Some(poll_exited));

                // Make sure we despawn last, so that other threads can only spawn the task
                // after we're done with it.
                this.raw.state.despawn(); // &= !STATE_SPAWNED

                #[cfg(feature = "trace")]
                trace::task_end(exec_ptr, &p);
            }
            Poll::Pending => {}
        }

        // the compiler is emitting a virtual call for waker drop, but we know
        // it's a noop for our waker.
        mem::forget(waker);
        // This comment refers to a specific optimization to avoid the overhead of Dynamic Dispatch (vtable lookup) 
        // on resource-constrained embedded CPUs like the ESP32-C3.
        // Here is the breakdown of what is happening:
        // 1. The "Virtual Call" Problem
        // A Rust Waker is essentially a "Fat Pointer" containing:
        //  1 A data pointer (to the TaskHeader).
        //  2 A pointer to a vtable (a table of function pointers for wake, drop, etc.).
        // When a Waker goes out of scope, the compiler normally generates code to look up the drop function in that 
        // vtable and call it. This is a virtual call. Even if the function it calls does nothing (a no-op), the CPU 
        // still has to perform the memory loads and the branch to execute that lookup.
        // 2. "Our Waker" is a No-Op
        // In Embassy, tasks are usually stored in static memory (using TaskStorage). Since the task memory never 
        // actually goes away (it lives for the duration of the program), the drop implementation for an Embassy waker 
        // is empty—it literally does nothing because there is no heap memory to free.
        // 3. The mem::forget(waker) Hack
        // By calling mem::forget(waker), the developer is telling the compiler: "Do not run the destructor for this 
        // object."
        // - Standard Rust: Usually, mem::forget is used to prevent a resource (like a Box or File) from being cleaned 
        //   up, potentially causing a leak.
        // - Embassy's Optimization: Since the Embassy developers know that the drop function is a no-op, they use 
        //   mem::forget to manually suppress the destructor.
        // - The Result: The compiler completely removes the code that would have performed the vtable lookup and the 
        //   virtual call. This saves a few instructions and a few cycles of CPU time every time a waker is handled, 
        //   which adds up in a high-frequency async executor.
        // Summary
        // The comment means: "We are skipping the 'Drop' logic for the Waker to save CPU cycles, because we know for a 
        // fact that our specific Waker doesn't have any resources to clean up anyway."
    }
}




/// Wake a task by `TaskRef`.
///
/// You can obtain a `TaskRef` from a `Waker` using [`task_from_waker`].
// 578  
pub fn wake_task(task: TaskRef) {
    let header = task.header();
    header.state.run_enqueue(|l| {
        // We have just marked the task as scheduled, so enqueue it.
        unsafe {
            let executor = header
                .executor
                .load(Ordering::Relaxed)
                .as_ref()
                .unwrap_unchecked();
            executor.enqueue(task, l);
        }
    });
}
// Logically, a task should never be woken if it hasn't been spawned. However, the code uses unwrap_unchecked() because, 
// while logically impossible, the type system doesn't know that.
// 1. The "Orphaned" Waker Problem
// In async Rust, a Waker is a cloneable object. It is possible for a peripheral (like a UART or Timer) to hold a Waker 
// from a previous attempt to poll a task.
// - If a task is cancelled, dropped, or re-initialized, but an interrupt still has a copy of the old Waker, that 
//   interrupt might call wake().
// - If the task header has been wiped or is in an uninitialized state (null executor pointer), calling wake() would 
// dereference null.
// 2. Why unwrap_unchecked instead of just "trusting" it?
// If the authors used a raw pointer cast &*header.executor.load(...), they would be performing a "blind" dereference.
// - In the 2026 Rust safety culture, as_ref().unwrap_unchecked() is the preferred way to say: "I know the type system 
// thinks this could be null, but I have a manual proof that the spawn() sequence has already completed."
// - It effectively moves the burden of proof to the spawn function. If wake is called and the pointer is null, the bug 
// actually happened in spawn (for not setting it) or the peripheral (for waking a dead task), but unwrap_unchecked 
// allows the wake function itself to be as fast as possible (zero branches).
// 3. The "Check-and-Branch" Overhead
// if you use standard Rust methods to handle a potential null (like unwrap() or match), the compiler must insert a 
// branch instruction into your ESP32-C3 machine code:
//   1 Load the pointer.
//   2 Compare pointer to zero.
//   3 Branch to a panic handler if it is zero.
//   4 Continue with the logic if it is non-zero.
// In a high-performance async executor, wake_task is called constantly. Multiplying that "check-and-branch" by every 
// wake-up in every task adds up to significant CPU cycle waste and increased code size.
// 4. "Panicking" vs. "Hardware Faulting"
// - Panic (unwrap()): This is a software-controlled crash. It requires the "Panic" infrastructure, which involves 
//   printing to the console and unwinding (if enabled). This takes up a lot of Flash and RAM.
// - Hardware Fault (unwrap_unchecked()): By telling the compiler "this will never be null," the compiler generates no 
//   check. If the pointer is null, the CPU will simply try to read address 0x0. The ESP32-C3 hardware will detect this 
//   "illegal" memory access and trigger a LoadProhibited/StoreProhibited exception.
// The Result: You still get a crash (the hardware fault), but you didn't have to pay the "CPU tax" of checking for it 
// in software every single time.
// 3. The Compiler "Hint"
// unwrap_unchecked() provides a powerful optimization hint to the LLVM backend:
// - It allows the compiler to assume the pointer is valid.
// - The compiler can then reorder instructions or keep values in registers more aggressively because it doesn't have 
//   to worry about the "early exit" path that a potential Panic would create.


// embassy/embassy-executor.me/src/raw/run_queue_critical_section.rs
use critical_section::{CriticalSection, Mutex};
// embassy-executor relies on the critical-section crate for its internal synchronization, rather than the Mutex in 
// embassy-sync, is primarily to avoid circular dependencies and to maintain universal hardware compatibility.
// 1. Avoiding Circular Dependencies
// The embassy-sync crate depends on embassy-executor for some of its async functionality. If embassy-executor were 
// to depend on embassy-sync for its own internal task-management mutex, it would create a circular dependency that 
// the Rust compiler cannot resolve.
// 2. Universal Hardware Abstraction
// The critical-section crate is a widely-adopted community standard that provides a single, unified way to disable 
// interrupts or acquire hardware spinlocks across different architectures.
// - Minimal Footprint: critical-section is extremely lightweight and does not require async support.
// - Low-Level Safety: The executor needs to synchronize its internal task queues at a very low level (even before 
// the async runtime is fully ready). The critical-section mutex provides a "blocking" lock that works safely across 
// different interrupt priorities and even between different CPU cores on chips like the ESP32-S3.

// The architectural split between SyncExecutor and the high-level Executor in embassy-executor exists to separate 
// thread-safe task management from architecture-specific waiting logic.
// 1. The Role of SyncExecutor (The "Core")
// The SyncExecutor is the "pure logic" engine. It contains the task queue and the polling state machine.
// - Why Sync?: It is designed to be Sync so it can be stored in a static variable. This allows the Spawner to access 
//   it from any thread or interrupt level to add new tasks.
// - Platform Agnostic: It does not know how to wait. It only knows how to poll tasks and manage the "run queue."
// - The Pender: It holds a reference to a "Pender," which it calls whenever a task becomes ready.
// 2. The Role of Executor (The "Wrapper")
// The Executor (e.g., embassy_executor::Executor) is a wrapper around SyncExecutor that is specialized for a specific 
// hardware architecture (like the ESP32-C3).
// - The "Wait" Logic: This is the layer that implements the run() loop. It tells the CPU to sleep (e.g., wfi or wait 
//   instruction) and handles the wake-up signal from the Pender.
// - Architecture Specific: On the ESP32-C3, the Executor is what ties the "Machine Software Interrupt" or the "Wait 
//   for Interrupt" logic to the task queue.
// 3. Why the Wrap is Necessary
// A. Separation of Concerns
// If SyncExecutor included the "Wait" logic, it would be tied to one specific CPU. By wrapping it, the same SyncExecutor 
// code can be used on ARM, RISC-V, and even WASM, while the outer Executor handles the hardware-specific sleep modes.
// B. The !Send Guard
// Executor includes a not_send: PhantomData<*mut ()> field.
// - The Logic: While the internal SyncExecutor must be Sync to allow tasks to be added from anywhere, the actual 
// execution loop (run()) must be pinned to one specific core or priority level.
// - The Result: The wrapper ensures that you cannot move a running executor to another thread, even though the internal 
//   task queue is thread-safe for adding work.
// C. Lifecycle Management
// The SyncExecutor handles the "Static" lifetime of the tasks. The Executor wrapper provides the user-friendly API for 
// the application developer to initialize the arena and start the loop.
